summary: Specifies a standard method of encapsulating IP datagrams on NetBIOS networks, so IP traffic can travel over such networks.

eli5.summary: Some networks only know how to carry one kind of envelope. This says how to tuck Internet packets inside that kind of envelope so they can be delivered.

questions: encapsulate ip datagrams on netbios networks
how are netbios names built from ip addresses
what is the mtu for ip over netbios
subtitle: How to carry IP datagrams inside NetBIOS datagrams by turning IP addresses into NetBIOS names.

tldr.problem: Hosts on a NetBIOS network need a compatible way to send IP datagrams, so that IP-based applications work there.
tldr.mechanism: Each IP datagram is sent as the data of a NetBIOS datagram. A host's NetBIOS name is built from its IP address, so no address lookup such as ARP is needed.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard. Broadcast uses a NetBIOS group name, multicast is not supported, and the MTU is 512 bytes.

today: RFC 1088 is an Internet Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1088 specifies a standard way to encapsulate Internet Protocol (RFC 791) datagrams on NetBIOS networks, so that independent implementations interoperate. NetBIOS can create virtual circuits and send point-to-point, multicast and broadcast datagrams, but this specification uses only the datagram services.

The RFC notes that earlier versions used the NetBIOS broadcast datagram service for IP broadcasting instead of NetBIOS group names, and that those versions are now obsolete. A router that can also encapsulate IP in ordinary data-link protocols such as 802.3 lets NetBIOS hosts reach the wider Internet.
sections.eli5: It is a rule book so everybody puts Internet packets into NetBIOS envelopes the same way.

sections.title: Address Mappings
sections.content:
NetBIOS names can be any series of 16 bytes. For IP applications, the name is chosen from the host's IP address: IP.XX.XX.XX.XX, where each XX is the ASCII hexadecimal form of one byte of the address.

Because the name is simply a mapping of the IP address, no physical address query mechanism such as ARP is needed. The RFC adds that this makes it easy to check an address by eye.
sections.eli5: Your mailbox label is made straight from your street number, so nobody has to look you up in a phone book.

sections.title: Broadcast, Multicast and MTU
sections.content:
The IP broadcast address is represented by the NetBIOS group name IP.FF.FF.FF.FF. No attempt is made to support IP multicast addresses with NetBIOS group names.

The maximum data size of a NetBIOS datagram, and so the MTU for IP over NetBIOS, is 512 bytes. Hosts talking to a NetBIOS host may therefore have to reassemble fragmented datagrams.
sections.eli5: Shouting to everyone uses one special name. Each envelope is small, so big messages are cut into pieces and put back together.

sections.title: Implementation Steps
sections.content:
To support IP for an address, start-up code must add IP.XX.XX.XX.XX to the NetBIOS name table, add IP.FF.FF.FF.FF to the group name table, and submit a receive datagram request for each of the two names. After each datagram arrives, another receive request is submitted.

An IP datagram is sent as NetBIOS datagram data with a send datagram request to either the host name or the broadcast name. Adapter status queries are optional, though the RFC says they may become mandatory as SNMP support becomes a requirement. When IP support stops, pending receives should be cancelled and both names deleted.
sections.eli5: Put your name on the mailbox, listen for mail, and take the name off when you move out.
